title: What does the fall of Icarus, son of Daedalus, teach us?
subtitle: The flight too close to the sun
subject: mythologie
description: Daedalus builds wings of wax to escape Crete. His son Icarus flies too high, falls, and gives his name to a sea. A myth about measure and excess.

hero.hook: A father invents wings. A son ignores the warning. The sea still carries his name.

blocks.text: Around 1560, a Flemish painter makes a picture called *Landscape with the Fall of Icarus*. It is one of the most famous paintings of the myth. There is just one problem.

blocks.caption: Where is Icarus? Take a second to look.

stops.text: Where is Icarus? Take a second to look.
**A farmer** ploughs his field, eyes on the ground.
**A shepherd** leans on his staff and stares at the sky. He is looking the wrong way.
**A ship** sails on, sails full of wind. It has somewhere to be.
**And there he is.** Two bare legs, kicking in the green water. The boy who flew is drowning, and nobody has noticed.
To understand how he got there, we have to go back to the beginning. It starts with his father.

blocks.text: His name is **Daedalus**, and he is the cleverest craftsman in Greece. He works for Minos, king of the island of Crete. For him, he builds the [[Labyrinth]]: a maze to hold a monster, the [[Minotaur]].

blocks.caption: Knossos, on Crete. This real palace, more than 3,500 years old, had hundreds of rooms on several floors. It may have inspired the legend of the maze.

blocks.text: Daedalus knows the maze's secret. So when a young hero finds his way out of it, Minos blames the inventor. He locks Daedalus and his son, **Icarus**, inside a tower. The king controls the land and the sea. There is no way off the island.
Minos watches the land and the sea. What is **left**? “He may block the land and the sea,” says Daedalus in Ovid's poem, “but the sky is open.” He starts collecting feathers.
blocks.prompt: Minos watches the land and the sea. What is **left**?
blocks.explanation: “He may block the land and the sea,” says Daedalus in Ovid's poem, “but the sky is open.” He starts collecting feathers.

blocks.text: He lays the feathers in a row, from the shortest to the longest. He ties the middle with thread and fixes the base with wax. Then he bends the whole thing into a gentle curve, like a real bird's wing.

blocks.caption: The take-off, painted in 1799. Daedalus gives his son a last push. Icarus is already looking at the sky, not at his father.

blocks.text: Before they leave, the father gives the son one rule. “Fly in the middle. Too low, and the sea spray will weigh down your feathers. Too high, and the sun will melt the wax.”
He warns against both. Too low is as dangerous as too high. People remember the sun and forget the sea, but the lesson was about staying in between.
blocks.prompt: Daedalus only warns his son about flying **too high**.
blocks.explanation: He warns against both. Too low is as dangerous as too high. People remember the sun and forget the sea, but the lesson was about staying in between.

blocks.text: They jump from Crete and head north, over the open sea. Fishermen and shepherds look up and take them for gods. Icarus is thrilled. He forgets the rule and climbs, higher and higher. The sun softens the wax. The feathers come loose. He falls here. The Greeks named the place after him. The island is still called Icaria, and the water around it the Icarian Sea. Daedalus buries his son and flies on alone, all the way to Sicily. He never uses his wings again.

steps.text: They jump from **Crete** and head north, over the open sea. Fishermen and shepherds look up and take them for gods.
Icarus is thrilled. He forgets the rule and climbs, higher and higher. The sun softens the wax. The feathers come loose. He falls **here**.
The Greeks named the place after him. The island is still called **Icaria**, and the water around it the Icarian Sea.
Daedalus buries his son and flies on alone, all the way to **Sicily**. He never uses his wings again.

blocks.caption: A painter from the 1600s chooses the exact second it goes wrong.

stops.text: A painter from the 1600s chooses the exact second it goes wrong.
**Icarus** tumbles backward, arms open. Around his shoulders, the wings are coming apart.
**Daedalus** turns his head. His own wings still hold. He can see everything, and do nothing.

blocks.text: He survives, and that is the cruel part. The inventor's creation works perfectly. It is his own son who pays for it.
blocks.prompt: In the myth, Daedalus **dies** in the fall too.
blocks.explanation: He survives, and that is the cruel part. The inventor's creation works perfectly. It is his own son who pays for it.

blocks.text: For the Greeks, the lesson is clear. Icarus is guilty of [[hubris]]: he wanted to rise as high as the gods. The story warns young people to listen, and everyone to know their limits.
Later centuries read it differently. For many poets and painters, Icarus becomes a hero: the one who dared, and who touched the sun before he fell.

blocks.caption: In 1898, the fallen boy has become a hero. His wings are whole and magnificent, and sea nymphs weep over him.

blocks.text: Back to the first painting. What is **Bruegel** telling us by hiding Icarus in a corner? The farmer ploughs, the ship sails, the sun shines. A Flemish proverb says: “No plough stops for a dying man.” It is one of the hardest readings of the myth.

blocks.text: A maze, a prison, an escape, a fall. The story has been retold for more than two thousand years.

blocks.explanation: A maze, a prison, an escape, a fall. The story has been retold for more than two thousand years.

blocks.text:
Daedalus, a brilliant inventor, escapes from Crete with his son on wings of feathers and wax.
His rule was to fly in the middle: not too low, not too high. Icarus climbs, the wax melts, and he drowns.
The Greeks saw a warning against pride. Later artists saw a hero who dared.
